\chapter{Hoy Como en Casa --- The Pieces That Move}
\label{ch:hoy-como}
\hlchaptermodality{265}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can move when and where around a sentence, and use the front for emphasis.}

I can move when and where around a sentence, and use the front for emphasis.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hoy como en casa]{hoy como en casa — the pieces that move}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-hoy-como-en-casa}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Como en casa.} — I eat at home. Now add \emph{hoy}, and put it wherever sounds right to you.

Whatever you chose was probably correct, and that is the lesson.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three placements, one meaning}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Hoy}} \emph{como en casa.} \emph{Como} \emph{\textbf{hoy}} \emph{en casa.} \emph{Como en casa} \emph{\textbf{hoy}}.
\end{quote}

All three are Spanish, and all three mean the same thing. The pieces that say \textbf{when} and \textbf{where} are not pinned to a position the way the subject and the verb are.

You can stack them, too: \emph{Hoy como en casa con María.} When, where, with whom — and the order among them is yours.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The freedom is not free, and it is not decoration. \textbf{The front of the sentence is the emphatic position.} Putting \emph{hoy} first says \emph{today}, as against some other day. Leaving it at the end mentions it and moves on.

So the choice is not stylistic. It is how a Spanish speaker does what an English speaker does by stressing a word out loud.

And notice why this is possible at all. The verb ending already says who is acting, and the personal \emph{a} already marks who is on the receiving end — so nothing depends on position to keep the roles straight. Latin's endings paid for word order when they fell; the pieces Spanish kept are what let the rest move.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all three placements of \emph{hoy}
  \item \emph{Hoy como en casa} as though correcting somebody about the day
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which position is the emphatic one? (The \textbf{front}.)

And what makes the freedom safe? (The \textbf{endings} already say who is doing what.)
\end{tcolorbox}
